$comment: Published engine artifacts, and the hashes that make them safe to reuse.
Read by ports/lib/fetch-engine.mjs, which downloads each file, checks its size and sha256
against this table, and only then puts it in place. Every sha256 here was computed from the
bytes of a real, tested build of the upstream commit recorded in `upstream`. If a file is
rebuilt, its hash changes and this entry must be updated to match.
Nothing enforces that. The publish workflow writes a manifest.json alongside the release assets
and does not touch this file, because a hash can only be known once the build it describes has
finished -- so this table is updated by hand from the published release's own manifest.json
(`gh release download <tag> -p manifest.json`). Two consequences worth knowing: a stale entry
does not fail loudly, it makes the fetch report exit 3 and fall back to a source build; and a
release is re-published under the same tag whenever the pinned upstream commit moves, so a pin
bump is not finished until this table has been re-read from the new release.
WHICH BUILD THESE DESCRIBE, AND WHY IT MATTERS
The `ons` entry describes the Linux runner's build, not a Windows dev-box build. Those two
are NOT byte-identical: emscripten 6.0.9 no longer has a working DETERMINISTIC setting, so a
build's function order, data-segment order and JS `dynCall_*` order all depend on the host.
Measured: `onsyuri.wasm` 4,660,610 B from the runner vs 4,660,612 B locally, with a different
function-index permutation. The two are behaviourally identical -- same canvas, same rendered
pixels, same shim state in a real browser -- but a hash cannot tell you that.
So the hash can only pin ONE build environment, and it must pin the producer's: the runner is
what creates the release, and a manifest describing anything else would make every fetch fail
verification (exit 3) and fall back to a source build -- silently defeating the feature. Three
independent runner builds were compared and were byte-identical, so the runner is reproducible
in a way a mixed fleet of dev machines is not.
`krkr` is pinned to the runner for the same reason, but there the two builds are further apart
(~17 KB in the wasm) because the vcpkg host triplets differ: the Windows recipe configures with
-DVCPKG_HOST_TRIPLET=x64-mingw-static while the runner uses the Linux default, so host-side ports
compile differently and the module ends up with two extra functions. What decides behaviour is
identical either way: `vlfs.js`, which carries the host byte-source seam, is byte-identical to the
tested Windows build; `index.html` and `shell.html` become identical once CRLF and the version
string are normalised; the seam patcher's two probes are asserted during the CI build; and the
runner runs upstream's own web tests. The build version is the 12-char upstream commit rather
than a per-run id, which is what makes these bytes pinnable at all.
`repository` + `releaseTag` give the download URL: <repository>/releases/download/<releaseTag>/<name>.
The tag convention is engine-<engine>-<version>. The repository is PRIVATE, so a release asset
answers an unauthenticated request with 404 -- set GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN and the helper falls
back to the release API to resolve the asset. The `artemis` entry has no release at all and is
not expected to get one: its engine links a proprietary SDK, so publishing it is a deliberate
opt-in (`publish_artifacts` / `ARTEMIS_PUBLISH_ARTIFACTS`). Until a release exists, a fetch on a
machine that does not already have the file reports it as unavailable (exit 2) and the caller
falls back to building from source.
AND THE TRAP INSIDE THAT OPT-IN: the `artemis` entry below describes a local Windows build, so
turning `ARTEMIS_PUBLISH_ARTIFACTS` on does not by itself make fetches work -- it publishes
runner-built bytes that do not match the entry, which then fail verification (exit 3) and fall
back to a source build, i.e. exactly the failure this file exists to prevent. Whoever enables it
must also replace the `artemis` hashes with the ones from the release it just created.
